transcript.speech: I kept getting this one comment on my loading videos. Why are you building loaders? Just make your app fast enough so you don't need one. So let's address this.
As a developer, there's a lot that you can do to speed up an application and overall make it a much better experience for your user.
But you could implement every strategy and it might not matter because you don't control all the things that are going to determine how fast it actually feels for the user.
Maybe the user is on a subway with two bars, or on bad hotel Wi-Fi.
Maybe your app uses Stripe for payment, and Stripe is having issues today so the payments are coming through slower.
So 'just make it fast' assumes every single thing goes right: fast device, strong signal, cooperation of other company's servers. But you can't count on that.
What you can do is you can think about what the user is thinking when things are slow and out of your control.
If you don't show anything, they're not going to think 'why is this so slow?' They're going to think 'This page is not working! What is happening?'
You don't build loaders instead of making something fast. You make things fast and you also plan for all the moments that you cannot control.
And if you want me to break down the ways that you speed up an app with development, which is a whole another series that I could do, comment and let me know.

creator_derived_lessons.creator_statement_paraphrase: Developers must optimize applications for performance while simultaneously implementing loading states to handle external factors beyond their control (e.g., weak network connection, third-party API delays).
creator_derived_lessons.visual_evidence: A graphic card displaying a red cross next to 'You don't build loaders instead of making something fast' followed by a green checkmark next to 'You make things fast, and you also plan for all the moments that you cannot control.'
creator_derived_lessons.ux_problem: When network or third-party service latency occurs and no loading indicator is shown, users assume the application is broken rather than simply loading.
creator_derived_lessons.recommended_change: Design and implement loading indicators alongside core performance optimizations to provide feedback during unavoidable delays.
creator_derived_lessons.specific_visual_or_interaction_change: Include visual indicators (skeleton loaders, spinners, progress bars) during asynchronous data fetching or background operations.
creator_derived_lessons.creator_reasoning: Developers cannot control external variables like user signal strength or third-party API latency; without feedback, users perceive a blank or unresponsive UI as a system failure.
creator_derived_lessons.applicable_context: Web and mobile applications dependent on network requests or third-party services.

analyst_interpretation.interpretation: The video highlights the psychological role of feedback in user interface design. Even when technical optimization is prioritized, perceived performance and system status visibility (Nielsen's first usability heuristic) remain essential to prevent user frustration during unexpected network or service delays.
inferences_not_shown_or_said: The video does not provide technical code examples for implementing specific loading state patterns like skeleton screens vs. spinners.
